title: Ramp Height and Cart Speed — Data Analysis (CER)
license: Original; data constructed to be consistent with v ≈ k·√h (ideal v = √(2gh) with modest, roughly constant fractional loss to friction). CC-BY 4.0 The Sovereign Academy.

answer_key.2: Curve rising and flattening (concave down), not a straight line through the origin.
answer_key.3: Speed increases with release height, but less than proportionally (doubling height does not double speed).
answer_key.5: Higher release → more gravitational potential energy (GPE ∝ height) → more of it is transferred to kinetic energy at the bottom (in an ideal, frictionless model all of it; in the real cart a roughly constant fraction is lost to friction and air resistance). Because KE depends on speed squared, doubling the energy multiplies speed by about √2 ≈ 1.4, not 2. (Grade-8 acceptable: 'the energy doubles but the speed does not, because kinetic energy grows faster than speed'.)
answer_key.6: Disagree. Pattern shows ×≈1.4 per doubling; 80 cm ≈ 2.60 × 1.4 ≈ 3.7 m/s, not 5.2.
answer_key.7: ≈ 2.9 m/s by extrapolation just beyond the measured range (accept 2.85–2.95 with a method: √(50/40)·2.60 ≈ 2.91, or extending a smooth curve; a straight-line extension giving ≈2.95 is acceptable if the student notes the curve is flattening). Credit the stated method and the acknowledgement that 50 cm lies outside the data.

contract.learning_target: Releasing the cart from higher up gives it more gravitational potential energy, which is transferred to kinetic energy on the way down (all of it in an ideal frictionless model; most of it in the real cart). Because kinetic energy depends on speed squared, speed grows roughly with the square root of release height — it increases with height but not proportionally to it.
contract.required_thinking: Compute and graph averages; identify a non-linear pattern from the numbers (compare ratios, not just 'it goes up'); construct a claim supported by specific data; explain the pattern with an energy-transfer model; use the pattern to evaluate a proportional-reasoning misconception and to extrapolate a prediction just beyond the measured range, stating the method.
contract.required_evidence: Correct averages; a labelled graph; a claim sentence; at least two quoted data comparisons including the two doublings; reasoning that names GPE→KE transfer and the speed-squared relationship in some grade-appropriate form; an explicit disagreement with the 'twice as fast' claim backed by the ×1.4 pattern; a prediction near 2.9 m/s for 50 cm with a stated method (extrapolation).
contract.teacher_constraints: 30 minutes; paper; graph sketched by hand; CER format for Part 2.

notes_for_reviewer: The difficult part is item 6 — recognising that the data contradict proportional reasoning. Item 7 is extrapolation (50 cm is beyond the measured 10–40 cm), and the method matters more than the number. A Support version that changes the data to be linear, or tells students 'notice speed does not double', has removed the construct. Items 1–2 are procedural on purpose; Support may reduce them (e.g. pre-fill two of four averages) without touching the CER. Correctness gate: any regenerated numbers must be recomputed and stay consistent with the √h pattern; any energy statement must not claim all GPE becomes KE in the real cart without naming the ideal model.

pass_looks_like: Averages partially pre-filled (e.g. 10 cm and 30 cm) so students still practise the computation but spend time on the CER; graph axes pre-drawn and scaled.
CER sentence frames that structure ('When the height went from ___ to ___, the speed went from ___ to ___, which is ___ times as fast') without supplying the ×1.4 conclusion.
Vocabulary glossed: potential energy, kinetic energy, photogate, proportional.
Item 6 kept as an evaluation of the student's claim; item 7 kept as an extrapolation with a stated method.
violation_looks_like: Data altered to a linear pattern, or the table extended to include 50 cm or 80 cm (answers to 6/7 placed in the data).
Directions that state the relationship ('Speed increases by about 1.4 times each time height doubles').
Item 6 reduced to yes/no with no explanation, or item 5 reduced to 'name two kinds of energy'.

expected_audits.note: A Support version is not expected to resist AI; adversarial verdict is recorded, not judged, unless it triggers a repair that then breaks preservation.

pass_looks_like: Students derive the multiplicative rule themselves and test it (does 10→40 give ×2? 1.30×2 = 2.60 ✓) then generalise: 'what height gives 3.0 m/s?'.
Interacting variable: a second cart with twice the mass — predict and justify (same speed, more energy) — with the prerequisite GPE/KE ideas still central.
Ask what the data would look like with no friction and why the measured speeds fall short of the ideal; or ask for the trial spread as evidence quality.
Fewer procedural items; averages may be given.
violation_looks_like: Adding four more heights to average.
Requiring the formula v = √(2gh) with no reasoning (recall substituted for reasoning).

expected_audits.note: Advanced is judged on depth; adversarial recorded.

pass_looks_like: Prediction before computing: 'Before you average anything, predict: if height doubles, does speed double? Circle yes/no.' Then item 6 asks the student to compare with their prediction.
Item 7 requires showing the method (ratio, curve extension, or √ rule) — the method is what is graded, the number is checked; the student should note that 50 cm is outside the measured range.
A two-line verification: 'Check your 50 cm prediction against the 40 cm and 30 cm values — does it sit where the curve says it should?'
Personalised input acceptable: each student is assigned one 'mystery height' (45, 55, 60 cm) from a list with a teacher key.
violation_looks_like: A lab-notebook style log of every step.
'Do this in class with no devices' as the verification mechanism.
Grading burden doubled (e.g. a full explanation for every one of 12 averages).

expected_audits.note: Visible must not come back UNDERMINED after its one repair cycle; if it does, that is a finding about the mode, not the case.

fixtures.why: Personalised height, 'in your own words', 'do not copy the textbook', and an honesty signature look like AI-resistance. None of it changes the cheapest path: photograph the sheet, tell the AI your digit, ask for a 13-year-old's voice. The signal is undermined; the only thing that would have helped (a prediction before computing, a two-line in-class verification) is absent. Also a mode violation: the honesty statement is 'inconvenience confused with validity'.

expected_evidence.adversarial: cheapest_path mentions pasting/photographing the table and supplying the personal digit; cost trivial or low; repair_hint proposes a prediction-before-data or in-class verification, not detection
expected_evidence.preservation: note on the MUST-NOT 'confuse inconvenience with assessment validity' / 'claim to be AI-proof'
